21 Wed Oct 28 - Parameter estimation with maximum likelihood We have mentioned previously in class that taking the logarithm of the response variable is not desirable and that maximum likelihood parameter estimation is an alternative in these situations. For a model of exponential growth, i.e., such as the increase in the number of COVID-19 cases at the start of the outbreak, historically, the logarithm of the response variable for the model has been applied so that the relationship between the predictor variables and the response variables are linear. Specifically, the exponential growth model is, \[ N_t = N_0 e^{rt} \] where \(N_t\) (units: number) is the size of the population at time \(t\), \(N_0\) is the initial population size (units: number), \(r\) is the net reproduction number (units: days\(^{-1}\)) and \(t\) is time in days relative to a reference date (i.e., when the population size was \(N_0\)). Exponential growth is a good model for population biology when population sizes are small (and this includes populations of infected people, such as the application to infectious diseases). We can take the logarithm of both sizes of this non-linear model to make the relationship betwen the logarithm of the response variable and the predictor variables be linear. Specifically, \[\begin{equation} \begin{array}{ccc} \ln(N_t) & = & \ln(N_0) + \ln(e^{rt}), \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{N_t}{N_0}\right) &=& rt. \\ \end{array} \end{equation}\] Given this transformation, we choose \(\ln\left(\dfrac{N_t}{N_0}\right)\) as our response variable (where \(N_0\), the initial population size has a known value) and then if we forced the regression intercept to 0, the slope of the regression, with \(t\) as the explanatory variable, is \(r\). We could implement such a regression to estimate \(r\), the net reproduction number of the population, but in taking the logarithm of both sides we have changed our assumptions about the residuals being normally distributed. In doing this transformation, now the residuals around \(\ln\left(\dfrac{N_t}{N_0}\right)\) are normally distributed, and relative to a response variable of \(N_t\) our estimate of \(r\) might be inaccurate. To avoid transforming our response variable we can fit the non-linear model using maximum likelihood. 21.1 Write the model We wish to estimate the doubling time for SARS-CoV-2 for the model, \[ N_t = N_0 e^{rt}, \] where the doubling time is calculated as \(t_D = \ln(2)/r\). Therefore, to calculate the doubling time, we need to estimate \(r\) in the exponential growth model. Consider our data, which is the number of reported COVID-19 cases in Newfoundland and Labrador from February 5, 2021 to February 12, 2021. require(dplyr) # This code involves a bit of data cleaning, but at the end our data is printed. COVID.data = read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ahurford/NL-public-COVID-data/main/NL_prov_stats.csv") dates <- COVID.data$date_of_update COVID.data$date_of_update <- format(as.POSIXct(dates,format='%Y/%m/%d %H:%M:%S'),format='%Y/%m/%d') COVID.data = filter(COVID.data,date_of_update >= "2021/02/05")%>%filter(date_of_update <= "2021/02/12")%>%select(date_of_update, new_provincial_cases) date = seq(as.Date("2021/02/05"), as.Date("2021/02/12"), "days") COVID.data <- data.frame(COVID.data, date)%>%mutate(t = seq(1,8))%>%rename(cases=new_provincial_cases)%>%select(-date_of_update) COVID.data ## cases date t ## 1 1 2021-02-05 1 ## 2 3 2021-02-06 2 ## 3 1 2021-02-07 3 ## 4 11 2021-02-08 4 ## 5 30 2021-02-09 5 ## 6 53 2021-02-10 6 ## 7 100 2021-02-11 7 ## 8 50 2021-02-12 8 Let’s graph our COVID-19 data to inspect whether fitting an exponential growth model to these data is reasonable. require(ggplot2) g1=ggplot(COVID.data, aes(x = t, y = cases)) + geom_point()+xlab("Days since February 5, 2021")+ylab("New reported COVID-19 cases")+theme_classic()+ggtitle("Alpha variant oubreak in Newfoundland and Labrador") g1 There is quite a bit of error deviation from exponential, likely due to undetected cases and reporting delays. Nonetheless, we will complete our analysis as a starting point. We will also assume that \(N_0 = 1\). 21.1.1 Writing the likelihood function Likelihood. Given the data, how likely is a parameter in the model. Can be contrasted with probability, where if the parameters are known, we can calculate the probability of an outcome. The likelihood function is, \[ L(\theta | y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i, n(t_i, \theta|\theta)). \] and the log-likelihood is, \[\begin{equation} \begin{array}{lll} LL(\theta | y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n) & = & \log\left(\prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i, n(t_i, \theta|\theta))\right),\\ & = & \sum_{i=1}^n \log\left(p(y_i, n(t_i, \theta|\theta))\right). \end{array} \end{equation}\] To write the likelihood function we need to make an assumption about our residuals. These case numbers are small, so we might choose the Poisson distribution. The Poisson distribution only has one parameter, so fitting this model involves one less complication than assuming normally distributed errors, where the normal distribution has both a mean and a variance parameter. Therefore, I will complete this example assuming a negative binomial distribution of errors. I am going to complete my model fitting using the mle2 function from the bbmle package. require(bbmle) ?mle2 Using this function requires me to create a function that returns the negative log-likelihood. This function depends on two parameters that I wish to estimate, \(r\) and the overdispersion parameter in the negative binomial, which is size. N0 <- 1 # fix N0 = 1 nLL = function(r,size){ nLLi=NULL #preallocation for(i in seq(1,length(COVID.data$t))){ t=COVID.data$t[i] Nt=COVID.data$cases[i] mu = N0*exp(r*t) # the model-predicted value for time, t. nLLi[i] = -log(dnbinom(Nt,mu = mu,size=size)) # this is the negative log-likelihood for the observation made at time t, given the model, for a particular choice of r, and the overdispersion. } nLL = sum(nLLi) } I can check my function supplying some values of r and size. test.val = nLL(r=1,size=2) test.val ## [1] 44.20782
